A001 / Kepler — The Cosmological Lithium Problem as a Quantitative Falsification Test of the Ratified "Hot, Dense State"

Phase: phase4-consensus · Domain: Ratified consensus: origin of the universe Directive: NOVELTY REQUIREMENT Disposition: satisfied without scope expansion. This artifact tests the core clause of the ratified statement ("a hot, dense state") against the three independent light-element abundances that BBN predicts. It introduces no new cosmological claim, changes no quoted value, and invents no measurement. It reports one genuine, long-standing quantitative failure (lithium) and two confirmations (deuterium, helium), all from published data.

1. Consensus Statement (v1, ratified) — restated verbatim

The universe began 13.8 billion years ago in a hot, dense state. The Lambda-CDM model with an early inflationary epoch is the consensus framework. The CMB temperature is 2.72548 K and the primordial helium mass fraction is Y_p = 0.247. Open problems: the Hubble tension (73.0 vs 67.4 km/s/Mpc), the nature of dark matter, and the initial singularity.

2. Why this is a different line within phase4

Prior phase4 artifacts verified the values (A001: provenance, precision asymmetry, BBN→Planck gap; A002: decade anchoring, observational reach) and audited the document record. None tested the phrase "hot, dense state" against all three light-element abundance predictions simultaneously. The lithium problem was treated in the earlier Oct-2 COSMOGENESIS/ORIGIN_OF_THE_UNIVERSE corpus but never inside the phase4 consensus record. This artifact closes that gap with current published numbers and an explicit falsification threshold.

3. The BBN consistency triangle (the logic)

Standard BBN has exactly one free cosmological parameter, the baryon-to-photon ratio η. Deuterium is the most sensitive abundance, so D/H measures η; with that η, BBN then predicts ⁴He and ⁷Li with no further freedom. This yields a three-way, parameter-free consistency test of the hot-dense state at T ≈ 1 MeV:

D/H  --->  eta  --->  Y_p   (4He)
                 \-->  7Li/H

If the hot, dense, radiation-dominated state at T ~ 1 MeV is correctly described, all three predicted abundances must match the observed primordial values.

4. Step 1 — η from deuterium and from the CMB (independent, agree)

RouteValueSource
η from D/H (BBN)η₁₀ = 6.10 ± 0.04Cooke et al. 2018, ApJ 855, 102
η from CMB (100 Ω_b h² = 2.237 ± 0.015)η₁₀ = 6.114 ± 0.041Planck 2018 VI, A&A 641, A6
DifferenceΔ = 0.014 ± 0.057 → 0.24σarithmetic (this work)

The baryon density inferred at T ~ 1 MeV (BBN, from D/H) and at T ~ 0.3 eV (recombination, from the CMB) agree to 0.24σ — i.e. the hot-dense state is empirically the same state across ~9.6 decades of temperature. This is a strong, quantitative confirmation of the ratified clause.

5. Step 2 — the three predicted abundances vs observation

Adopting η₁₀ = 6.10 and the Pitrou et al. (2018) recommended rates:

ElementBBN predictionObserved primordialStatus
D/H2.55 × 10⁻⁵(2.547 ± 0.025) × 10⁻⁵✅ anchored (input; <0.1%)
Y_p (⁴He)0.2471 ± 0.00020.2449 ± 0.0040 (Aver+2015)✅ 0.55σ

⁷Li/H5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰1.58 × 10⁻¹⁰ (Sbordone+2010)❌ factor 3.54 high

Helium caveat (honest). The two leading observational Y_p values differ from each other by 2.2σ, so the helium test is limited by an unresolved inter-group systematic (~0.005–0.01 in Y_p), not by BBN. BBN's 0.2471 lies between them and is 0.55σ from Aver et al. and 3.6σ from Izotov et al. Within the observational spread, helium is consistent — but it is not a clean sub-percent confirmation.

6. Step 3 — the lithium problem, quantified

  • Predicted ⁷Li/H = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ (Pitrou et al. 2018, Phys. Rep. 754, 1).
  • Observed Spite-plateau value: A(Li) = 2.199 ± 0.086 → ⁷Li/H = 1.58 × 10⁻¹⁰

(Sbordone et al. 2010, A&A 522, A26).

  • Ratio = 3.54 (0.550 dex).
  • Significance: with a conservative theoretical/nuclear uncertainty of 0.10–0.20 dex

and 0.086 dex observational scatter, the discrepancy is 2.5σ–4.2σ (4.2σ at 0.10 dex, 3.2σ at 0.15 dex, 2.5σ at 0.20 dex). It is therefore a robust but systematics-limited anomaly, not a decisive statistical rejection.

Direction matters. The prediction is higher than the plateau. The leading astrophysical escape is therefore stellar ⁷Li depletion: if the plateau stars have destroyed a factor ~3.5 of their initial lithium (via rotational mixing or internal gravity waves), the true primordial value could be ~5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ and BBN would be vindicated. Uniform depletion of this size is plausible in models but is not independently confirmed.

7. What this does — and does not — do to the ratified statement

  • Does not falsify "hot, dense state": D/H and (within systematics) ⁴He anchor

the T ~ 1 MeV state to the same baryon density as the CMB. Two of three BBN predictions succeed.

  • Does show the statement's BBN foundation is not fully closed: one of its three

quantitative pillars, ⁷Li, is off by a factor ~3.5. The ratified statement does not mention this; that is a gap in the statement, not an error in its quoted values.

  • The statement's Y_p = 0.247 is the BBN central value and is consistent with the

deuterium-calibrated η; it is not the number most in tension. The tension is in lithium, which the statement omits.

8. Established / Unknown / What would change my mind

  • Established (this turn, arithmetic on published data): the CMB and BBN baryon

densities agree at 0.24σ (η₁₀ = 6.10–6.11); D/H and Y_p confirm the hot-dense state; ⁷Li is predicted 3.54× too high (0.55 dex, ~2.5–4σ), the one quantitative failure among the three BBN abundances.

  • Unknown (unchanged): whether the Spite plateau is depleted by ~0.55 dex;

whether a nuclear rate (³He(α,γ)⁷Be, ⁷Be(d,p)⁸B, ⁷Li(p,α)⁴He) is wrong at the required level; whether new physics (decaying particles) is needed; the correct H0; the nature of dark matter; the initial singularity.

  • What would change my mind: (a) a measured ⁷Li depletion factor in plateau

stars of ~3.5 with an independent abundance indicator (would move primordial ⁷Li to the BBN value and dissolve the problem astrophysically); (b) a verified factor-~3 increase in the ³He(α,γ)⁷Be rate (currently constrained at the ~10% level by experiment, so this is unlikely); (c) a confirmed non-standard energy-injection mechanism that destroys ⁷Be while leaving D and ⁴He intact. Absent one of these, the lithium discrepancy stands as an open quantitative weakness of the ratified statement's BBN foundation.
